previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a complex history including Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, SVC syndrome, and PTSD was admitted with facial swelling and acute-on-chronic right upper quadrant abdominal pain. Imaging revealed a clot in the superior vena cava extending toward the right atrium, managed with Argatroban initially and transitioned to warfarin. Due to her history of HIT, heparin was avoided. Her abdominal pain was attributed to a Crohn’s flare, and she was treated with a non-allergenic antibiotic. Pain and anxiety were managed with Dilaudid, Oxazepam, and Benadryl. Her symptoms improved, INR stabilized, and she was discharged home on warfarin, Cipro, and adjusted psychiatric medications with follow-up arranged. No surgical intervention was required.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with a previously placed malfunctioning Port-a-
Cath.

RADIOLOGISTS:  The procedure was performed by Drs. ___, the
attending radiologist who was present and supervising throughout.  Dr. ___
___ the exam.

PROCEDURE AND FINDINGS:  After informed consent was obtained from the patient
explaining the risks and benefits of the procedure, the patient was placed
supine on the angiography table and the right neck and the left groin were
prepped and draped in standard sterile fashion.  A preprocedure timeout was
performed.  General anesthesia was administered throughout the procedure.

Using sterile technique, local anesthesia and ultrasound guidance, attempts to
obtain intravenous access using the left femoral approach were performed
without success with a 21 gauge micropunture needle.

It was then decided to use the right internal jugular venous approach.  Using
sterile technique, local anesthesia and ultrasound guidance, the right
internal jugular vein was punctured and a 0.018 Glidewire was advanced through
the needle under fluoroscopic guidance.  Hardcopy ultrasound images were
stored before and after the puncture.  The needle was then exchanged for a
micropuncture sheath. The wire and the inner dilator of the sheath were
removed and a venogram was performed through the sheath demonstrating complete
occlusion of the SVC with the presence of collaterals at this level.  The
micropuncture sheath was exchanged over the wire for a 6 ___ vascular
sheath. Based on the diagnostic findings, it was decided to recanalize the SVC
and perform balloon angioplasty.  Recanalization of the SVC was performed with
a combination of a Kumpe catheter and a 0.035 Super Stiff Glidewire.  The wire
was advanced through the SVC into the right atrium under fluoroscopic
guidance.  Using a combination of the Kumpe catheter and a Glidewire access
was obtained within the IVC.

Balloon angioplasty was performed at the level of the SVC with 6, 8 and 10 mm
regular balloons, with good results.  At this point, contrast material was
injected through both lumens of the previously placed Port-a-Cath
demonstrating signs of presence of a fibrin sheath around the distal part of
the catheter.  Based on these findings it was decided that the patient would
benefit from stripping of the fibrin sheath which was performed with a snare
device.

Contrast material was injected through both ports of the Port-a-Cath
demonstrating good flow through the catheter.  Blood could be aspirated
through both ports without difficulty.

The patient tolerated the procedure well without immediate complications and
was transferred to the PACU in good condition.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Occlusion of the SVC with successful recanalization and balloon
angioplasty of the SVC with 6, 8 and 10 mm regular balloons.

2.  Successful stripping of a fibrin sheath surrounding double lumen chest
port catheter.
